newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam approves fewer foreign investment projects.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam approves fewer foreign investment projects.

text.p: Vietnam reported on Sunday that foreign investment approvals had slowed so far this year, but quoted a government official as saying billions of dollars in potential new projects lay just around the corner.

The official Vietnam News Agency (VNA) said the Ministry of Planning and Investment (MPI) had licensed 118 new foreign-invested projects worth $1.3 billion between the beginning of January and the end of May.
It did not give comparative figures for the same period in 1996 but said the amount of capital involved was lower, although investment in production had risen.

The report went on to detail several major projects approved in recent months, including a $100 million brewery in the northern province of Nghe An and a $130 million Industrial Zone near Ho Chi Minh City.
"Some projects with combined capital of billions of U.S. dollars are under consideration by the MPI," VNA quoted deputy MPI Minister Nguyen Nhac as saying, adding:
"He (Nhac) predicted that the number of projects to be granted with investment licences in the coming time may be smaller than last year but total invested capital will be higher."
In 1996, foreign investment levels reached a record level of around $9 billion, although critics said the figures were helped by a flurry of approvals in the last few days of the year.
Vietnam's communist government opened the country's doors to foreign investors in the late 1980s. By the end of last year it had received pledges worth $27.3 billion towards some 1,687 projects.
But only around $10 billion of that total has actually been committed.

The past year has seen a slowdown in the number of projects being approved. Government officials say this reflects Vietnam's new determination to focus on the quality rather than quantity of investment coming from overseas.

Analysts say the figures also reflect investor fatigue with Vietnam, where problems such as red-tape, a weak infrastructure, corruption, high hidden-costs and a shifting regulatory environment are seen as having dented enthusiasm.
